# What Is an Open Line System (OLS)?


November 20th, 2026


An open line system, or open optical line system (OLS), is the optical line layer of a dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) network, deployed and managed as its own system so that it can carry wavelengths generated by other vendors' equipment. It holds the amplifiers, multiplexer/demultiplexer (mux/demux) filters and reconfigurable optical add/drop multiplexers (ROADMs). The transponders that create the wavelengths sit outside it, and the operator can buy them separately.


### Closed DWDM systems versus Open Line Systems (OLS)


DWDM increases fiber capacity by transmitting multiple data streams simultaneously, each on a different wavelength of light.


In the traditional model, one vendor supplies the line equipment, the transponders and the management system, all linked through proprietary interfaces. That vendor also owns network planning. According to the Telecom Infra Project (TIP), closed DWDM systems rely on vendor-specific wavelength planning tools, leaving operators with limited insight into how planning decisions are made.


An open line system decouples the optical transport infrastructure from the transponders and muxponders.


TIP's white paper[Target Architecture: Disaggregated Open Optical Networks](https://cdn.mediavalet.com/usva/telecominfraproject/VdNAxFBh8UKdTtvU_OOU2A/ooMkKLHdL0i-qq-fgsIxvQ/Original/TIP_OOPT_MUST_Optical_Whitepaper_Target_Architecture_-_Disaggregated_Open_Optical_Networks__v10_-_GREENPUBLIC_ACCESS.pdf) was co-signed by eight operators, including Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone. It calls a system open when it exposes application programming interfaces (APIs) with a well-known, standard protocol, model and rules that operators can build into their own networks and operations systems. Under that definition, an open line system accepts any optical signal that meets its interface specification and exposes a programmable northbound API.


### Line equipment and terminal equipment


Line equipment makes up the OLS:


- **Optical amplifiers** , including in-line amplifiers placed in long fiber spans to make up for signal loss.
- **Mux/demux filters** , which combine wavelengths onto one fiber and separate them at the far end.
- [ROADMs](https://ribboncommunications.com/company/media-center/blog/what-roadm) , which route individual wavelengths to add, drop or pass-through ports without converting them to electrical signals.


Terminal equipment generates the wavelengths:


- **Transponders** , which map one client signal onto one line-side wavelength.
- **Muxponders** , which multiplex several client signals onto a single wavelength.
- **Routers and switches** with built-in DWDM line interfaces.


The two parts of the network age at different speeds. TIP's paper says a new generation of coherent DWDM transponders arrives on average every two years, while DWDM line systems have an average lifecycle of 10 years. A highway and its traffic follow the same pattern: the road is built to last decades, while vehicle designs change every few years. Separating terminals from the line lets the operator adopt the most suitable and cost-efficient transponders as they appear. Amplifiers and ROADMs with years of service left stay in place.


### How an open line system works


#### Alien wavelengths


A wavelength generated by one vendor's transponder and carried over another vendor's line system is called an[alien wavelength](https://ribboncommunications.com/company/media-center/blog/alien-wavelengths-shared-spectrum) , a practice that is becoming commonplace. Operators use them to migrate from one vendor to another and to mix transponders from several vendors. The line system's mux port filters and power monitoring keep an alien wavelength from disturbing the channels next to it.


Equipment from different vendors can only work together if they share a definition of the single-channel interface between terminal and line. TIP points to two efforts. The first is[ITU-T G.698.2](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-G.698.2) , the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T) Recommendation for amplified multichannel DWDM applications with single-channel optical interfaces. The second is the W interface of the Open ROADM Multi-Source Agreement (MSA).


#### Flexgrid channel allocation


[ITU-T G.694.1](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-G.694.1) defines the DWDM frequency grid.[IETF RFC 7698](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7698.html) from the Internet Engineering Task Force summarizes its flexible grid as follows:


- Channel center frequencies sit in 6.25 GHz steps from a 193.1 THz anchor.
- Each slot is a multiple of 12.5 GHz wide.
- This replaces the fixed channel spacing of fixed-grid networks, which is typically 50 GHz.


A flexgrid line can give a high-rate signal a wide slot and a lower-rate signal a narrow one, so lower rate channels do not waste spectrum.


#### Open APIs and SDN control


A software-defined networking (SDN) controller is what lets operators manage equipment from several vendors as one network. In TIP's target architecture, the optical SDN domain controller covers both the line and third-party terminals: discovery, provisioning, fault monitoring and performance monitoring. The operators chose two sets of interfaces:


- **Northbound (from the controller to higher systems):** the Open Networking Foundation (ONF) Transport API (T-API).
- **Southbound (from the controller to terminals):**[OpenConfig](https://github.com/openconfig/public/tree/master/release/models/optical-transport) data models over NETCONF and the gRPC Network Management Interface (gNMI).


OpenConfig publishes models in the YANG data modeling language for terminal devices, optical amplifiers, wavelength routers and channel monitors. The[Open ROADM MSA](https://github.com/OpenROADM/OpenROADM_MSA_Public) publishes optical specifications along with device, network and service models.


#### Degrees of openness


Aspect Closed system Partially disaggregated Fully disaggregated


Line equipment Single vendor One vendor, integrated as a single OLS Each element (amplifiers, mux/demux, ROADMs) managed individually


Terminals Single vendor Third-party terminals over the vendor's line Any vendor


Management Vendor proprietary interfaces One point of management for the OLS; open APIs to terminals SDN controller manages every network element


Integration and testing Single vendor OLS vendor integrates the line system Whoever integrates the line owns system design, optical power management and integration testing


TIP's operators chose partial disaggregation as their target. The paper expects it to be simpler to manage, because one vendor stays responsible for integrating the line system.


### Why Operators adopt Open Line Systems


**Wider supplier choice.** TIP notes that fewer vendors now offer integrated DWDM systems, because of consolidation and changes in focus. An open line system depends less on any single vendor, since line interfaces from different suppliers can share the same line.


**Upgrades without replacing the line.** An operator can add a newer generation of coherent transponders as alien wavelengths over amplifiers and ROADMs already in service. Ribbon calls this[staggered network evolution](https://learn.rbbn.com/hubfs/Corporate%20Marketing%20%28TOP%20LEVEL%29/Application%20Notes/AN%20Apollo%20Open%20Optical%20Networking.pdf) : transmission equipment is replaced on a faster cycle, and optical line systems stay in service longer.


**Capacity that grows with demand.** TIP's operators describe a pay-as-you-grow approach to capacity. They buy terminals as traffic requires and match each transponder to its route's rate and reach. Flexgrid slots are sized to fit each signal.


**Price competition.** Buying the line and the terminals separately puts each under competitive pressure, and TIP and Ribbon both count competition among the benefits. How much an operator saves depends on network scale and on how much integration work it takes on.


**One management view.** Standard APIs let a single controller provision and monitor the operator's own wavelengths and third-party wavelengths together. Planning becomes more open as well. TIP's GNPy is a vendor-independent, open-source application that checks the end-of-life margins of optical connections.


### Trade-offs Operators Should Weigh


TIP's operators acknowledge the costs:


- a more complex procurement process
- more responsibility for system integration
- more testing and evaluation
- more complex lifecycle and connection management across vendors


**Support accountability.** In a closed system, one vendor answers for every element. When a third-party transponder runs over another vendor's line, a fault can sit on either side of the boundary, and the operator must coordinate between suppliers.


**Interoperability testing.** In a bookended pair, one vendor supplies both ends of a wavelength and has already secured interoperability. In an interoperable pair, each end comes from a different vendor, which adds testing that the operator or its integrator carries.


**Integration and skills.** Not every line system controller can manage third-party terminals. For those cases, TIP describes adding a hierarchical SDN controller above the line controllers. Teams that integrate controllers themselves need engineers who are skilled with YANG models, NETCONF and controller workflows.


**Visibility into shared spectrum.** Leasing a band of spectrum, rather than a single wavelength, carries more risk if the host operator cannot see what the customer launches. Ribbon gives an example: one wavelength launched into a band set up for four can be over-amplified to 6 dBm and cause cross-phase modulation in other parts of the spectrum. Ribbon's Muse Multilayer Automation Platform can monitor the individual wavelengths in a leased band and control their power and gain. Ribbon also notes that the industry is still far from agreeing on how shared spectrum should be implemented and managed.


### Where Open Line Systems are Used


- **Data center interconnect (**[DCI](https://ribboncommunications.com/company/media-center/blog/what-data-center-interconnect-dci-complete-guide) **).** DCI links two or more data centers. The Optical Internetworking Forum (OIF) started its 400ZR project after large data center operators asked for an interoperable coherent interface. The[400ZR Implementation Agreement](https://www.oiforum.com/oif-publishes-implementation-agreement-for-400zr-coherent-optical-interface/) , published in April 2020, covers amplified point-to-point DWDM links of 120 km or less.
- **Cloud backbones.**[A 2018 study by Microsoft authors](https://opg.optica.org/jocn/abstract.cfm?uri=jocn-10-2-A216) tested switching platforms from three vendors that used the same coherent digital signal processor (DSP) chipset. Over Microsoft's open line system, they worked together across 2,000 km at 150G using 8QAM and across 1,000 km at 200G using 16QAM (quadrature amplitude modulation).
- **Operator mesh networks.** TIP's target architecture covers meshed networks and point-to-point DCI across one or several line system domains. Where wavelengths cross more than one vendor's line, a hierarchical SDN controller manages them.
- **Routers with coherent optics.**[Coherent routing](https://ribboncommunications.com/company/media-center/blog/what-coherent-routing) puts coherent optical transceivers directly into IP routers. Pluggables such as 400G ZR+ fit router ports. An optional OLS with mux/demux and amplifiers combines the wavelengths and extends their reach.
- **Wholesale spectrum.** With alien spectral pipes, an operator gives a customer a point-to-point band of spectrum to run its own wavelengths. Ribbon names large enterprises, data center operators and other network operators as possible customers.


### Open Line Systems from Ribbon


Ribbon Communications offers a disaggregated optical line system. Under the theme "No Lock-in", it describes its[optical networking](https://ribboncommunications.com/solutions/service-provider-solutions/optical-networking) portfolio as "disaggregated systems with open standard interfaces." Key value propositions Ribbon identifies for its Apollo and Muse solutions:


- **Third-party wavelengths:** The[Apollo open optical line system](https://ribboncommunications.com/products/service-provider-products/apollo-optical-networking/open-optical-line-systems) 9458 carries wavelengths from any router, switch or optical transport system. Ribbon applies provisioning, performance monitoring and dynamic Wavelength Switched Optical Network (WSON) restoration to third-party alien wavelengths as well.
- **Alien wavelength solutions:** Apollo's[coherent alien wavelength solutions](https://ribboncommunications.com/products/service-provider-products/apollo-optical-networking/apollo-alien-wavelengths) range from 100G to 1.2T. They can be controlled through an element management system (EMS) or an OpenConfig API, and they are field-proven over third-party optical line systems.
- **Alien spectrum:** The Apollo OLS extends alien wavelengths to alien spectrum, through spectral pipes and spectral slicing.
- **Degrees of disaggregation:** Ribbon supports both partially and fully disaggregated networks based on OpenConfig and OpenROADM APIs.
- **Control:** The[Muse Multilayer Automation Platform](https://ribboncommunications.com/products/service-provider-products/muse-multilayer-automation-platform) is a cloud-native multilayer domain controller for IP/Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and optical transport. It supports third-party equipment for unified visibility, topology management and alarm monitoring.
